newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Bonn empowers shareholders, limits banks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bonn empowers shareholders, limits banks.

text.p: The German government on Tuesday unveiled a bill aimed at broadening shareholder rights, limiting the power of banks, and increasing corporate transparency and accountability.
The draft legislation is an attempt to improve Germany's shareholder culture, in which banks are seen to exercise great power at the expense of small shareholders.
The bill is aimed squarely at strengthening Germany's role as an international financial market, and the attractiveness of German companies to foreign investors.
"We must orient our corporate law more strongly toward international capital markets," Justice Minister Edzard Schmidt-Jortzig told a news conference.
"The importance of foreign investors and their expectations is increasing. German issuers stand in direct competition with other seekers of risk capital throughout the world," the draft bill says.
The debate on the bill within Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet was stimulated by some spectacular corporate failures such as Metallgesellschaft AG, Bremer Vulkan AG, and KHD AG.
But no amount of legislation could prevent the kind of management errors that occured in those cases, economics minister Guenter Rexrodt told the same news conference.
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) attacked the draft bill, saying it made too many concessions to the vested interests of banks and insurance companies.
SPD parliamentarian Hans Martin Bury said an SPD-sponsored alternative bill would go further to limit the role such institutional investors could play in corporate management.

The government bill, based on Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition pact, will be opened to public debate in January, and should be ready for cabinet approval in early spring so that it could take effect January 1998, Schmidt-Jortzig said.

Even within the coalition, controversy continues. The bill aims to limit the seats on supervisory boards, which are made up of non-executive directors, to 12 in most cases. Some politicians see this as a bid to limit the power of unions.

Labour unions control half the seats on supervisory boards in Germany, a practice known as "Mitbestimmung." Rexrodt said the custom would be maintained, despite friction it causes with other European countries.
"In the Anglo-Saxon world, Mitbestimmung is seen as something shocking, but we think it has proved its worth. We have some convincing to do," Rexrodt said.
The draft legislation would bar banks from exercising proxies on shares deposited with them, if they are also exercising votes on their own holdings that total more than five percent of the company.
The bill would also ease rules on corporate share buybacks in line with European Union guidelines.

Bonn plans to eliminate the multiple voting rights enjoyed by some shareholders, which allow local governments to exercise control of utility RWE AG, for example, though they hold a minority of the shares.

It will also eliminate the ceilings on maximum voting rights, which have been used by some companies as a takeover defence, by limiting the voting rights a single shareholder may exercise, even if he holds more shares.
The draft law would also sharpen Bonn's supervision of companies' advisory boards and limit the number of such posts a single director may hold.
